claim: A mouse ortholog of NORAD (2900097C17Rik or Norad) exhibits 61% nucleotide identity with its human counterpart.
source: A mouse ortholog of NORAD (2900097C17Rik or Norad), exhibiting 61% nucleotide identity with its human counterpart, is clearly identifiable on mouse chromosome 2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the nucleotide identity percentage between mouse and human NORAD orthologs.

claim: Mouse Norad shows minimal protein-coding potential as assessed by PhyloCSF.
source: Like the human transcript, mouse Norad shows minimal protein-coding potential as assessed by PhyloCSF, a metric that discriminates between coding and noncoding sequences based on their evolutionary signatures (Lin et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: PhyloCSF analysis data is referenced and shown in a figure, with citation to the PhyloCSF method.

claim: Both human and mouse NORAD/Norad are ubiquitously expressed throughout the body, with highest abundance in brain.
source: Both human and mouse NORAD/Norad are ubiquitously expressed throughout the body, with highest abundance in brain (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Expression data across tissues is presented in figures showing brain has highest expression.

claim: Mouse Norad shows predominately cytoplasmic localization in mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: RNA fluorescent in situ hybridization (RNA FISH) in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), as well as fractionation experiments in a panel of mouse cell lines, revealed a predominately cytoplasmic localization of Norad (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), mirroring the localization of the human transcript (Lee et al., 2016; Tichon et al., 2016).
evidence: RNA FISH and fractionation experimental data are presented in figures, with citation to prior work on human transcript.

claim: Norad-deficient mice were viable, fertile, and born at the expected Mendelian frequency.
source: Norad–/– mice were viable, fertile, and born at the expected Mendelian frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Mendelian frequency data is presented in a supplementary figure showing expected ratios.

claim: By 6 months of age, Norad-deficient mice showed onset of a multi-system degenerative phenotype resembling premature aging.
source: Early in life, Norad-deficient mice were indistinguishable from wild-type littermates, but by 6 months of age, the onset of a multi-system degenerative phenotype resembling premature aging became apparent, with approximately 50% of the mice developing severe manifestations by 1 year of age (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Phenotypic observations over time are documented with figures showing aging-related changes.

claim: Male Norad-deficient mice showed accelerated alopecia and graying of fur.
source: This phenotype was characterized by accelerated alopecia and graying of fur in male Norad–/– mice (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Photographic evidence of alopecia and fur graying is shown in figures.

claim: Both male and female Norad-deficient mice displayed pronounced kyphosis.
source: while both male and female Norad–/– mice displayed pronounced kyphosis (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Kyphosis scoring data and images are presented in figures for both sexes.

claim: Increased kyphosis was evident in Norad+/– animals, indicating a dose-dependent effect of Norad loss of function.
source: Increased kyphosis was also evident in Norad+/– animals, indicating a dose-dependent effect of Norad loss of function.
evidence: Comparison of kyphosis scores across genotypes shows dose-dependent relationship.

claim: Norad-deficient mice that developed kyphosis exhibited significant weight loss accompanied by loss of total body fat and subcutaneous fat.
source: Although body weight was comparable between cohorts of Norad+/+, Norad+/–, and Norad–/– mice at 1 year of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), mice that developed outward features of aging such as kyphosis also exhibited significant weight loss accompanied by loss of total body fat and subcutaneous fat (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Body weight, fat percentage, and subcutaneous fat thickness measurements are presented in figures.

claim: Norad-deficient skeletal muscle showed marked switching of fast twitch glycolytic (FTG) fibers to slow twitch oxidative (STO) fibers.
source: Abnormalities were also apparent in Norad-deficient skeletal muscle, with marked switching of fast twitch glycolytic (FTG) fibers to slow twitch oxidative (STO) fibers (Figure 2F), a phenomenon associated with normal muscle aging (Ciciliot et al., 2013).
evidence: Muscle fiber type analysis data is presented in a figure, with citation linking this to normal aging.

claim: Norad-deficient mice showed accelerated onset of aging-associated pathologies within the central nervous system, including condensed neuronal cell bodies and accumulation of lipofuscin and vacuoles within spinal motor neurons.
source: In addition, Norad–/– mice showed accelerated onset of aging-associated pathologies within the central nervous system (CNS) (Gray and Woulfe, 2005; Samorajski et al., 1968; Son et al., 2012), including condensed neuronal cell bodies and an accumulation of lipofuscin and vacuoles within spinal motor neurons (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Histological data showing CNS pathologies is presented in figures, with citations to prior work on aging-associated CNS changes.

claim: Norad-deficient mice showed an overall reduction in neuronal density in the spinal cord.
source: These changes were accompanied by an overall reduction in neuronal density in the spinal cord (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Quantification of neuronal density is presented in a supplementary figure.

claim: Norad-deficient mice showed decreased overall survival over a 2-year interval.
source: Finally, Norad–/– mice showed decreased overall survival over a 2-year interval (Figure 2H).
evidence: Survival curve data over 2 years is presented in a figure.

claim: Norad is essential to suppress widespread aging-associated degenerative phenotypes in mice.
source: These findings demonstrate that Norad is essential to suppress widespread aging-associated degenerative phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the multiple aging phenotypes observed in Norad-deficient mice.

claim: Mouse Norad harbors 11 perfect matches to the canonical PRE consensus and an additional 3 PREs conforming to a slightly relaxed consensus sequence.
source: Like human NORAD, the mouse transcript is highly enriched for PREs, harboring 11 perfect matches to the canonical PRE consensus and an additional 3 PREs conforming to a slightly relaxed consensus sequence (UGUANAUN) (Figure 3A).
evidence: PRE sequence analysis is shown in a figure mapping PRE locations on Norad.

claim: Norad was the most highly bound PUM2 target in the mouse brain transcriptome.
source: Accordingly, robust binding of PUM2 to Norad was detectable by eCLIP, with the majority of binding occurring in the vicinity of PRE sequences. Strikingly, Norad was by far the most highly bound PUM2 target in the transcriptome (Figure 3B), exhibiting at least 1000 times greater CLIP signal than 95% of all PUM2-bound mRNAs.
evidence: eCLIP data showing Norad as the top PUM2 target is presented in a figure.

claim: Norad is the preferred RNA target of PUM2 in mouse brain.
source: Thus, as observed in human cell lines, but to a much greater extent in vivo, Norad is the preferred RNA target of PUM2 in mouse brain.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the eCLIP data showing Norad as the most highly bound target.

claim: PUM2 target occupancy was significantly increased in Norad-deficient brain.
source: To estimate the apparent PUM2 CLIP signal for each target in Norad+/+ and Norad–/– brain, the average reads in CLIP clusters in a given target 3' UTR normalized to the expression level of the target was determined for each condition, an approach used previously to estimate relative binding in CLIP data (Bosson et al., 2014). This analysis suggested that PUM2 target occupancy was significantly increased in Norad–/– brain, consistent with PUMILIO hyperactivity (Figure 3C).
evidence: eCLIP analysis comparing PUM2 binding in wild-type vs knockout brain is presented, with citation to the analytical method.

claim: Expression of PUM2 CLIP targets was significantly decreased in Norad-deficient brain.
source: Further supporting this conclusion, RNA-seq revealed that expression of PUM2 CLIP targets was significantly decreased in Norad–/– brain (Figure 3D).
evidence: RNA-seq data comparing target expression levels is presented in a figure.

claim: Augmented repression of PUM2 CLIP targets was more apparent when examining targets whose PUM2 binding was measurably increased in the Norad-deficient condition.
source: Augmented repression of PUM2 CLIP targets was even more apparent when specifically examining targets whose PUM2 binding was measurably increased in the Norad–/– condition (Figure 3E).
evidence: Analysis of a subset of targets with increased PUM2 binding is presented in a figure.

claim: Norad functions as a negative regulator of PUMILIO activity in vivo.
source: Together, these data strongly support a conserved function for Norad as a negative regulator of PUMILIO activity in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the eCLIP and RNA-seq data showing increased PUM2 binding and target repression in Norad-deficient mice.

claim: There was a significant increase in aneuploid lymphocytes and splenocytes in 3-month and 12-month-old Norad-deficient mice.
source: To assess whether Norad loss of function results in genomic instability, DNA FISH was used to quantify the number of marker chromosomes in primary hematopoietic cells, a representative mitotic tissue. This analysis revealed a significant increase in aneuploid lymphocytes and splenocytes in 3-month and 12-month-old Norad–/– mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: DNA FISH data quantifying aneuploidy in hematopoietic cells is presented in a figure.

claim: There was a significant increase in aneuploidy in Norad-deficient MEFs.
source: To directly determine whether loss of Norad results in mitotic abnormalities, MEFs were examined using DNA FISH and live cell imaging. In contrast to lymphocytes or splenocytes, we observed a high rate of polyploidization in all MEF lines tested, as previously reported (Todaro and Green, 1963) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B). We therefore excluded tetraploid and octaploid cells from those scored as aneuploid (higher ploidy was rarely observed). Despite applying these stringent criteria, we detected a significant increase in aneuploidy in Norad–/– MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: DNA FISH data in MEFs is presented in a supplementary figure, with citation to prior work on MEF polyploidization.

claim: Time lapse microscopy revealed an increased occurrence of anaphase bridges and lagging chromosomes in Norad-deficient MEFs undergoing mitosis.
source: Moreover, time lapse microscopy revealed an increased occurrence of anaphase bridges and lagging chromosomes as Norad–/– MEFs underwent mitosis (Figure 4B).
evidence: Live cell imaging data showing mitotic defects is presented in a figure.

claim: Norad-deficient mouse tissues and cells exhibit genomic instability.
source: Thus, Norad-deficient mouse tissues and cells exhibit genomic instability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the DNA FISH and live imaging data showing aneuploidy and mitotic defects.

claim: RNA-seq revealed significant repression of genes required for mitosis, DNA repair, and DNA replication in Norad-deficient spleens.
source: In human cell lines with NORAD deficiency, genome instability has been linked to repression of a program of genes that are required for mitosis, DNA repair, and DNA replication due to PUMILIO hyperactivity (Lee et al., 2016). Consistent with these findings, RNA-seq revealed significant repression of a similar set of genes in Norad–/– spleens (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: RNA-seq data and gene ontology analysis is presented in figures, with citation to prior work in human cells.

claim: Brain PUM2 CLIP targets with two or more PREs in their 3' UTRs were downregulated in Norad-deficient spleens.
source: Moreover, brain PUM2 CLIP targets with two or more PREs in their 3' UTRs were downregulated in Norad–/– spleens, providing evidence of PUMILIO hyperactivity in this tissue (Figure 4E).
evidence: Analysis of PUM2 target expression in spleen is presented in a figure.

claim: The Norad-PUMILIO axis has a conserved, essential role in the maintenance of genomic stability in mammals.
source: Taken together, these data support a conserved, essential role for the Norad-PUMILIO axis in the maintenance of genomic stability in mammals.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genomic instability phenotypes and gene expression changes observed in Norad-deficient mice.

claim: Overt mitochondrial abnormalities were observed in skeletal muscle of 12-month-old Norad-deficient mice, including large accumulations of subsarcolemmal mitochondria.
source: Phenotypic analyses of Norad-deficient mice unexpectedly revealed that in addition to genomic instability, widespread mitochondrial dysfunction was evident in knockout tissues. Overt mitochondrial abnormalities were observed in skeletal muscle of 12-month-old Norad–/– mice, including large accumulations of subsarcolemmal mitochondria (Figure 5A–B)
evidence: Histological images showing mitochondrial accumulations are presented in figures.

claim: Norad-deficient skeletal muscle showed a significant increase in mitochondrial DNA content.
source: Overt mitochondrial abnormalities were observed in skeletal muscle of 12-month-old Norad–/– mice, including large accumulations of subsarcolemmal mitochondria (Figure 5A–B) accompanied by a significant increase in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) content (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: mtDNA quantification data is presented in a supplementary figure.

claim: Mitochondria in Norad-deficient skeletal muscle appeared irregular in shape and enlarged, with loss of cristae.
source: Ultrastructurally, these mitochondria appeared irregular in shape and enlarged, with loss of cristae (Figure 5B).
evidence: Electron microscopy images showing mitochondrial morphology are presented in a figure.

claim: Irregular and enlarged mitochondria were observed in spinal neurons of Norad-deficient mice.
source: Similarly irregular and enlarged mitochondria were observed in spinal neurons of Norad–/– mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Electron microscopy images of spinal neurons are presented in a figure.

claim: Norad-deficient mice showed decreased cytochrome c oxidase activity in spinal neurons.
source: These structural abnormalities were accompanied by evidence of reduced mitochondrial function, such as decreased cytochrome c oxidase (COX; also known as Complex IV of the electron transport chain) activity in spinal neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: COX histochemistry data is presented in a figure.

claim: Rare COX-negative fibers were observed in Norad-deficient but not wild-type skeletal muscle.
source: Additionally, rare COX-negative fibers were observed in Norad-deficient but not wild-type skeletal muscle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: COX histochemistry images of skeletal muscle are presented in a supplementary figure.

claim: Basal and maximal respiration was significantly reduced in Norad-deficient MEFs.
source: To directly assess mitochondrial function in Norad-deficient cells, respiration rates were analyzed in pairs of littermate-matched Norad+/+ and Norad–/– MEFs. Basal and maximal respiration was significantly reduced in Norad–/– cells (Figure 5E)
evidence: Seahorse analysis data measuring oxygen consumption rates is presented in a figure.

claim: Norad-deficient MEFs showed a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential and an increase in ROS production.
source: Basal and maximal respiration was significantly reduced in Norad–/– cells (Figure 5E), accompanied by a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) and an increase in ROS production (Figure 5F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data measuring MMP and ROS levels is presented in a figure.

claim: HCT116 cells lacking NORAD exhibited a significant increase in mitochondrial content.
source: Respiration was also examined in human NORAD–/– HCT116 cells (Lee et al., 2016). Unlike MEFs, HCT116 cells lacking NORAD exhibited a significant increase in mitochondrial content (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: mtDNA quantification data in HCT116 cells is presented in a supplementary figure, with citation to the cell line source.

claim: When normalized to mtDNA copy number, NORAD-deficient HCT116 cells showed a reduction in respiration and increase in ROS.
source: Nevertheless, when normalized to mtDNA copy number, a similar reduction in respiration and increase in ROS was detectable in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: Seahorse and ROS analysis data normalized to mtDNA content is presented in supplementary figures.

claim: Brain and spinal cord of Norad-deficient mice show evidence of oxidative damage, including elevated levels of 3-nitrotyrosine, 4-hydroxynonenal, and 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine/8-hydroxyguanosine.
source: A major consequence of mitochondrial dysfunction that is believed to play a role in cellular damage and aging is the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Raha and Robinson, 2000; Zorov et al., 2014). Indeed, brain and spinal cord of Norad–/– mice show evidence of oxidative damage, including elevated levels of 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT), 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), and 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine/8-hydroxyguanosine (8-OHdG/8-OHG), markers of protein, lipid, and nucleic acid oxidation, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry and ELISA data for oxidative damage markers is presented in supplementary figures, with citations to prior work on ROS and aging.

claim: Norad is required for the maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis in mammalian cells and tissues.
source: These results document a previously unrecognized requirement for Norad in the maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis in mammalian cells and tissues.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the multiple lines of evidence showing mitochondrial dysfunction in Norad-deficient cells and tissues.

claim: Genes associated with mitochondria-related gene ontology terms were significantly repressed in Norad-deficient brain and spleen.
source: To investigate the mechanism through which Norad loss-of-function leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, we examined RNA-seq data from Norad+/+ and Norad–/– brain and spleen using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005). Genes associated with mitochondria-related gene ontology (GO) terms, such as mitochondrial protein complex, electron transport chain, and oxidative phosphorylation, were significantly repressed in Norad-deficient tissues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data is presented in supplementary figures, with citation to the GSEA method.

claim: Identical mitochondria-related gene sets were repressed in human NORAD-deficient HCT116 cells.
source: Remarkably, identical gene sets were repressed in human NORAD–/– HCT116 cells.
evidence: Comparison of GSEA results between mouse and human knockout cells shows conservation of the phenotype.

claim: A set of PUM2 brain CLIP targets with important functions in mitochondrial biogenesis, homeostasis, transport, oxidative phosphorylation, metabolism, and ROS detoxification were identified.
source: We further identified a set of PUM2 brain CLIP targets within these gene sets that are known to perform important functions in mitochondrial biogenesis and homeostasis, mitochondrial transport, oxidative phosphorylation, metabolism, and ROS detoxification (Figure 6A).
evidence: A list of PUM2 targets with mitochondrial functions is presented in a figure based on CLIP data.

claim: Downregulation of mitochondrial PUM2 target genes was validated by qRT-PCR in Norad-deficient brain, spleen, and multiple independent MEF lines.
source: Downregulation of a representative set of these genes was validated by qRT-PCR in Norad–/– brain, spleen, and multiple independent MEF lines (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: qRT-PCR validation data is presented in figures.

claim: PUMILIO hyperactivity in Norad-deficient cells and tissues leads to coordinated downregulation of target genes critical for normal mitochondrial function.
source: These data are consistent with a model in which PUMILIO hyperactivity in Norad-deficient cells and tissues leads to coordinated downregulation of a broad set of target genes that are critical for normal mitochondrial function.
evidence: This mechanistic model is inferred from the gene expression and functional data.

claim: Administration of doxycycline induced broad transgene expression in Pum2; rtTA3 double transgenic mice.
source: To address this question, transgenic mice with doxycycline (dox)-inducible expression of FLAG-tagged PUM2 were generated and crossed to mice harboring a ubiquitously expressed reverse tetracycline-controlled transactivator 3 transgene (CAG-rtTA3) (Premsrirut et al., 2011) (Figure 7A). Administration of dox induced broad transgene expression in Pum2; rtTA3 double transgenic mice, as documented by FLAG immunohistochemistry (IHC) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: FLAG IHC data showing transgene expression is presented in a supplementary figure, with citation to the rtTA3 mouse line.

claim: RNA-seq of spleens from Pum2; rtTA3 transgenic animals revealed significant repression of PUM2 targets, demonstrating PUM2 hyperactivity.
source: Importantly, RNA-seq of spleens from transgenic animals revealed significant repression of PUM2 targets, demonstrating PUM2 hyperactivity in this tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis of PUM2 target expression is presented in a supplementary figure.

claim: Administration of doxycycline to young Pum2; rtTA3 double transgenic mice resulted in a striking phenotype within 2 months that closely resembled Norad-deficient mice at 1 year of age.
source: Administration of dox to young (8–14 week-old) Pum2; rtTA3 double transgenic mice derived from two independent founders, but not to Pum2 or rtTA3 single transgenic controls, resulted in a striking phenotype within 2 months that closely resembled the appearance of Norad–/– mice at 1 year of age.
evidence: Phenotypic comparison between Pum2 transgenic and Norad knockout mice is described.

claim: Dox-treated Pum2; rtTA3 mice developed rapidly progressing kyphosis, alopecia, graying of fur, and loss of body fat.
source: Dox-treated Pum2; rtTA3 mice developed rapidly progressing kyphosis, alopecia, graying of fur, and loss of body fat (Figure 7B–C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Phenotypic data for Pum2 transgenic mice is presented in figures.

claim: Dox-treated Pum2; rtTA3 mice showed increased aneuploidy in splenocytes.
source: These phenotypes were accompanied by increased aneuploidy in splenocytes (Figure 7D)
evidence: DNA FISH data showing aneuploidy in Pum2 transgenic splenocytes is presented in a figure.

claim: Pum2; rtTA3 skeletal muscle showed accumulation of subsarcolemmal, irregularly shaped mitochondria lacking normal cristae.
source: These phenotypes were accompanied by increased aneuploidy in splenocytes (Figure 7D) and the accumulation of subsarcolemmal, irregularly shaped mitochondria lacking normal cristae in skeletal muscle (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: Histological and electron microscopy images of Pum2 transgenic muscle are presented in figures.

claim: A global reduction in COX activity was observed in Pum2; rtTA3 skeletal muscle.
source: Further demonstrating mitochondrial abnormalities, a global reduction in COX activity was observed in Pum2; rtTA3 skeletal muscle (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: COX histochemistry data for Pum2 transgenic muscle is presented in figures.

claim: Pum2; rtTA3 skeletal muscle showed scattered necrotic and regenerating fibers.
source: Further demonstrating mitochondrial abnormalities, a global reduction in COX activity was observed in Pum2; rtTA3 skeletal muscle (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B) together with scattered necrotic and regenerating fibers (Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: H&E staining images showing muscle pathology are presented in figures.

claim: Transient expression of FLAG-PUM2 in MEFs significantly impaired respiration.
source: Lastly, we directly assessed whether enforced PUM2 expression impairs mitochondrial function in MEFs and human cell lines. Transient expression of FLAG-PUM2 in MEFs or stable expression of either PUM1 or PUM2 in HCT116 significantly impaired respiration (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Seahorse analysis data for PUM2-overexpressing MEFs is presented in figures.

claim: Stable expression of either PUM1 or PUM2 in HCT116 cells significantly impaired respiration.
source: Transient expression of FLAG-PUM2 in MEFs or stable expression of either PUM1 or PUM2 in HCT116 significantly impaired respiration (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Seahorse analysis data for PUM1/2-overexpressing HCT116 cells is presented in supplementary figures.

claim: PUMILIO hyperactivity in Norad-deficient animals results in genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, and a multi-system degenerative phenotype resembling premature aging.
source: Overall, these data provide compelling evidence that PUMILIO hyperactivity in Norad-deficient animals results in genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, and ultimately a multi-system degenerative phenotype resembling premature aging.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Pum2 transgenic mouse phenotypes that phenocopy Norad knockout.

claim: Deletion of Norad in mice results in genomic instability and mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to a dramatic multi-system degenerative phenotype resembling premature aging.
source: Here, we investigated the physiologic function of the conserved lncRNA Norad in vivo. Deletion of Norad in mice results in genomic instability and mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to a dramatic multi-system degenerative phenotype resembling premature aging.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the main findings.

claim: Loss of tissue homeostasis in Norad-deficient animals is attributable to augmented activity of PUMILIO proteins.
source: Loss of tissue homeostasis in Norad-deficient animals is attributable to augmented activity of PUMILIO proteins, which act as post-transcriptional repressors of target mRNAs to which they bind.
evidence: This mechanistic conclusion is stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Norad is the preferred RNA target of PUMILIO2 (PUM2) in mouse tissues.
source: Norad is the preferred RNA target of PUMILIO2 (PUM2) in mouse tissues and, upon loss of Norad, PUM2 hyperactively represses key genes required for mitosis and mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the eCLIP findings.

claim: Upon loss of Norad, PUM2 hyperactively represses key genes required for mitosis and mitochondrial function.
source: Norad is the preferred RNA target of PUMILIO2 (PUM2) in mouse tissues and, upon loss of Norad, PUM2 hyperactively represses key genes required for mitosis and mitochondrial function.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is stated in the abstract based on the eCLIP and RNA-seq data.

claim: Enforced Pum2 expression fully phenocopies Norad deletion, resulting in rapid-onset aging-associated phenotypes.
source: Accordingly, enforced Pum2 expression fully phenocopies Norad deletion, resulting in rapid-onset aging-associated phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the Pum2 transgenic mouse findings.

claim: NORAD is a recently described lncRNA that is distinguished by its high abundance in mammalian cells and strong evolutionary conservation across mammalian species.
source: Noncoding RNA activated by DNA damage (NORAD) is a recently described lncRNA that is distinguished from the majority of transcripts in this class due to its high abundance in mammalian cells and strong evolutionary conservation across mammalian species (Lee et al., 2016; Tichon et al., 2016).
evidence: This characterization of NORAD is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: NORAD functions as a strong negative regulator of PUMILIO1 (PUM1) and PUMILIO2 (PUM2) in human cells.
source: Studies in human cells have established that this RNA functions as a strong negative regulator of PUMILIO1 (PUM1) and PUMILIO2 (PUM2), RNA binding proteins (RBPs) that belong to the deeply conserved family of Pumilio and Fem3 binding factor (PUF) proteins.
evidence: This functional characterization is stated based on prior studies in human cells.

claim: PUM1/2 bind specifically to the eight nucleotide PUMILIO response element (PRE) (UGUANAUA), which is often located in the 3' UTR of mRNAs.
source: PUM1/2 bind specifically to the eight nucleotide (nt) PUMILIO response element (PRE) (UGUANAUA), which is often located in the 3' UTR of mRNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PUM1/2 binding specificity.

claim: Binding of PUM1/2 to PRE sites triggers accelerated deadenylation, reduced translation, and turnover of mRNA targets.
source: Binding of PUM1/2 to these sites triggers accelerated deadenylation, reduced translation, and turnover of mRNA targets (Miller and Olivas, 2011; Quenault et al., 2011).
evidence: This mechanism of PUM1/2 action is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: NORAD limits the availability of PUM1/2 to repress target mRNAs by binding a large fraction of PUM1/2 within the cell.
source: With the capacity to bind a large fraction of PUM1/2 within the cell, NORAD limits the availability of these proteins to repress target mRNAs (Lee et al., 2016; Tichon et al., 2016).
evidence: This mechanism is stated with citations to prior work on NORAD function.

claim: Inactivation of NORAD results in PUMILIO hyperactivity with augmented repression of target mRNAs including key regulators of mitosis, DNA repair, and DNA replication.
source: Consequently, inactivation of NORAD results in PUMILIO hyperactivity with augmented repression of a program of target mRNAs that includes key regulators of mitosis, DNA repair, and DNA replication.
evidence: This consequence of NORAD loss is stated based on prior work.

claim: Dysregulation of mitosis, DNA repair, and DNA replication genes results in dramatic genomic instability in NORAD-deficient cells.
source: Dysregulation of these genes results in dramatic genomic instability in NORAD-deficient cells (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citation to prior work in human cells.

claim: PUM2 overexpression is sufficient to phenocopy the NORAD knockout phenotype in human cells.
source: In accordance with this model, PUM2 overexpression is sufficient to phenocopy, while PUM1/2 loss-of-function is sufficient to suppress, the NORAD knockout phenotype in human cells.
evidence: This genetic interaction is stated based on prior work in human cells.

claim: PUM1/2 loss-of-function is sufficient to suppress the NORAD knockout phenotype in human cells.
source: In accordance with this model, PUM2 overexpression is sufficient to phenocopy, while PUM1/2 loss-of-function is sufficient to suppress, the NORAD knockout phenotype in human cells.
evidence: This genetic interaction is stated based on prior work in human cells.

claim: SAM68 interacts with NORAD and facilitates PUMILIO antagonism by this lncRNA.
source: Recent work has identified additional RNA-binding proteins that interact with NORAD including SAM68, which facilitates PUMILIO antagonism by this lncRNA (Tichon et al., 2018)
evidence: This interaction is stated with citation to recent work.

claim: RBMX is an RNA binding protein that interacts with NORAD and contributes to the DNA damage response.
source: Recent work has identified additional RNA-binding proteins that interact with NORAD including SAM68, which facilitates PUMILIO antagonism by this lncRNA (Tichon et al., 2018), and RBMX, an RNA binding protein that contributes to the DNA damage response (Munschauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This interaction is stated with citation to recent work.

claim: The emergence of NORAD specifically within mammals suggests the existence of strong selective pressure to maintain tight control of PUMILIO activity within this lineage.
source: Although PUF proteins are deeply conserved across eukaryotic species, the emergence of NORAD specifically within mammals suggests the existence of strong selective pressure to maintain tight control of PUMILIO activity within this lineage.
evidence: This evolutionary inference is drawn from the conservation patterns of PUF proteins and NORAD.

claim: In mice, PUM1 and PUM2 loss-of-function has been linked to behavioral abnormalities, elevated neuronal excitability, and impaired neurogenesis.
source: In mice, PUM1 and PUM2 loss-of-function has been linked to behavioral abnormalities, elevated neuronal excitability, and impaired neurogenesis, while inactivation of PUM1 reduces fertility in males and females (Goldstrohm et al., 2018).
evidence: These phenotypes are stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of PUM1 reduces fertility in male and female mice.
source: In mice, PUM1 and PUM2 loss-of-function has been linked to behavioral abnormalities, elevated neuronal excitability, and impaired neurogenesis, while inactivation of PUM1 reduces fertility in males and females (Goldstrohm et al., 2018).
evidence: This phenotype is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Mammalian neurons are exquisitely sensitive to reduced dosage of PUMILIO, with only a 25% to 50% reduction in PUM1 expression resulting in neurodegeneration in both human and mouse brain.
source: Interestingly, mammalian neurons are exquisitely sensitive to reduced dosage of PUMILIO, with only a 25% to 50% reduction in PUM1 expression resulting in neurodegeneration in both human and mouse brain (Gennarino et al., 2018; Gennarino et al., 2015).
evidence: This dosage sensitivity is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of the neighboring genes Epb41l1 and Cnbd2 was unaffected in Norad-deficient brain and spleen.
source: Importantly, expression of the neighboring genes Epb41l1 and Cnbd2 was unaffected in Norad–/– brain and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), demonstrating that deletion of the Norad locus does not perturb neighboring gene expression.
evidence: RNA-seq data for neighboring genes is presented in a supplementary figure.

claim: Deletion of the Norad locus does not perturb neighboring gene expression.
source: Importantly, expression of the neighboring genes Epb41l1 and Cnbd2 was unaffected in Norad–/– brain and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), demonstrating that deletion of the Norad locus does not perturb neighboring gene expression.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the RNA-seq data showing no change in neighboring gene expression.

claim: The relaxed PRE consensus was the most enriched sequence motif detected in PUM2-bound mRNA 3' UTRs.
source: We next examined the transcriptome-wide interactions of PUM2 with target mRNAs. Notably, the relaxed PRE consensus was the most enriched sequence motif detected in PUM2-bound mRNA 3' UTRs, supporting the reliability of this eCLIP dataset (Figure 3B).
evidence: Motif enrichment analysis of eCLIP data is presented in a figure.

claim: Genomic instability in mice causes aging-associated phenotypes.
source: Given the prior demonstration that genomic instability in mice causes aging-associated phenotypes (Baker et al., 2004; Baker et al., 2006), the regulation of PUMILIO activity by this lncRNA, and the resulting effects of PUMILIO hyperactivity, could potentially underlie the phenotype of Norad-deficient animals.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work linking genomic instability to aging.

claim: A decline in mitochondrial function is linked to aging-associated phenotypes.
source: These findings were noteworthy given the extensive evidence linking a decrease in mitochondrial function to aging-associated phenotypes (Sun et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review on mitochondrial function and aging.

claim: Mice lacking proofreading activity of the mtDNA polymerase accumulate mtDNA mutations and deletions and exhibit a premature aging phenotype with many similarities to Norad-deficient mice.
source: These findings were noteworthy given the extensive evidence linking a decrease in mitochondrial function to aging-associated phenotypes (Sun et al., 2016) and the previous demonstration that mice lacking proofreading activity of the mtDNA polymerase, which consequently accumulate mtDNA mutations and deletions, exhibit a premature aging phenotype with many similarities to that seen in Norad–/– mice (Trifunovic et al., 2004).
evidence: This comparison is made with citation to prior work on mitochondrial mutator mice.

claim: The budding yeast Puf family member Puf3p preferentially associates with mRNAs that encode mitochondrial proteins and facilitates their local translation in the vicinity of the mitochondrial protein import machinery.
source: The regulation of mitochondrial biogenesis and function by PUMILIO-related proteins is not restricted to mammals. The budding yeast Puf family member Puf3p preferentially associates with mRNAs that encode mitochondrial proteins and facilitates their local translation in the vicinity of the mitochondrial protein import machinery (García-Rodríguez et al., 2007; Gerber et al., 2004; Saint-Georges et al., 2008).
evidence: This function of yeast Puf3p is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila and cultured mammalian cells, PUMILIO proteins repress translation of mRNAs that encode mitochondria-destined proteins until these transcripts are docked at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: In Drosophila and cultured mammalian cells, PUMILIO proteins repress translation of mRNAs that encode mitochondria-destined proteins until these transcripts are docked at the mitochondrial outer membrane (Gehrke et al., 2015).
evidence: This mechanism is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: PUMILIO proteins have a deeply conserved role in the regulation of mitochondrial biology across eukaryotic species.
source: Together, these observations suggest a deeply conserved role for PUMILIO proteins in the regulation of mitochondrial biology across eukaryotic species.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the conservation of PUMILIO function in mitochondrial regulation across species.

claim: A recent RNA-seq study reported a strong age-related decrease in NORAD expression in the subependymal zone of human brains.
source: Remarkably, a recent RNA-seq study of noncoding RNA expression in the subependymal zone of human brains of increasing age reported a strong age-related decrease in NORAD expression (Barry et al., 2015).
evidence: This finding is stated with citation to a prior study.

claim: NORAD and PUMILIO proteins represent new candidates whose altered expression or function may influence the normal age-related decline in tissue function.
source: These findings take on added significance in light of our new understanding of the consequences of disruption of the Norad-PUMILIO axis and suggest that this lncRNA, and its target PUMILIO proteins, represent new candidates whose altered expression or function may influence the normal age-related decline in tissue function.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the age-related decrease in NORAD expression and the findings from this study.

claim: NORAD and PUMILIO genes represent previously unrecognized candidates that may be mutated or disrupted in rare progeroid cases unlinked to known progeroid genes.
source: These genes also represent previously unrecognized candidates that may be mutated or otherwise disrupted in rare progeroid cases that are unlinked to the genes that are presently known to cause these disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the premature aging phenotype observed.

claim: One major function of Norad is to buffer PUMILIO activity such that it stays within a critical range.
source: In light of these findings, we propose that one major function of Norad is to buffer PUMILIO activity such that it stays within this critical range.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings of PUMILIO dosage sensitivity.

claim: Norad is likely utilized for dynamic regulation of PUMILIO activity under selected conditions such as DNA damage and hypoxia.
source: In addition to providing a buffering function, it is likely that Norad is also utilized for dynamic regulation of PUMILIO activity under selected conditions. In particular, this lncRNA is known to be induced by a variety of cellular stressors, including DNA damage (Lee et al., 2016) and hypoxia (Michalik et al., 2014), which would be expected to result in de-repression of PUMILIO targets following these stimuli.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work showing Norad induction by stress, combined with inference about the functional consequences.

claim: Cells that are sensitive to enforced Pum2 expression likely include stem cell populations whose dysfunction could lead to loss of tissue homeostasis and degenerative phenotypes.
source: Cells that are sensitive to enforced Pum2 expression likely include stem cell populations whose dysfunction could lead to loss of tissue homeostasis and degenerative phenotypes. Accordingly, PUMILIO and related proteins have been implicated as critical stem cell regulators in model organisms and mammals (Crittenden et al., 2002; Forbes and Lehmann, 1998; Leeb et al., 2014; Lin and Spradling, 1997; Naudin et al., 2017; Shigunov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis with citations to prior work on PUMILIO in stem cells.

claim: A recent study reported that elevated PUM2 levels in aged mice impaired mitochondrial homeostasis.
source: These findings were corroborated by a recent study reporting that elevated PUM2 levels in aged mice impaired mitochondrial homeostasis (D'Amico et al., 2019).
evidence: This corroborating finding is stated with citation to a recent study.

claim: Mitochondrial mutator mice develop a premature aging phenotype with many features in common with Norad-deficient mice.
source: A large body of evidence has linked a decline in mitochondrial function to aging-associated phenotypes (Sun et al., 2016), including the direct demonstration that 'mitochondrial mutator mice', which harbor a mutation in the mitochondrial DNA polymerase and consequently accumulate mtDNA mutations, develop a premature aging phenotype with many features in common with Norad–/– mice (Trifunovic et al., 2004).
evidence: This comparison is made with citations to prior work on mitochondrial function and aging.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction in concert with genomic instability provides a compelling mechanistic basis for the phenotype of Norad-deficient animals.
source: Thus, mitochondrial dysfunction in concert with genomic instability, another abnormality associated with premature aging in mice (Baker et al., 2004; Baker et al., 2006), provides a compelling mechanistic basis for the phenotype of Norad-deficient animals.
evidence: This mechanistic conclusion is drawn from the observed phenotypes and prior work on aging, with citations.

claim: The Norad-PUMILIO axis is important in mammalian physiology and maintenance of homeostasis across tissues.
source: Our studies of the murine Norad ortholog reported here unequivocally establish the importance of this lncRNA, and the tight regulation of its target PUMILIO proteins, in mammalian biology and implicate the Norad-PUMILIO axis as a major regulator of aging-associated phenotypes (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on all the findings.

claim: The Norad-PUMILIO axis is a major regulator of aging-associated phenotypes.
source: Our studies of the murine Norad ortholog reported here unequivocally establish the importance of this lncRNA, and the tight regulation of its target PUMILIO proteins, in mammalian biology and implicate the Norad-PUMILIO axis as a major regulator of aging-associated phenotypes (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion based on all the findings.

claim: PUMILIO activity must be maintained within a very narrow range to prevent widespread deleterious consequences.
source: Taken together with our findings from this study, in which we examined for the first time the effects of mammalian PUMILIO hyperactivity in vivo, we can conclude that PUMILIO activity must be maintained within a very narrow range in order to prevent widespread deleterious consequences.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the findings of both PUMILIO deficiency and hyperactivity causing severe phenotypes.

claim: An RNA such as Norad represents an ideal molecule to serve as a buffer of PUMILIO activity, as it is able to efficiently regulate the activity of a pre-existing pool of PUMILIO at the level of target engagement.
source: Indeed, an RNA such as Norad represents an ideal molecule to serve as a buffer of this type, as it is able to efficiently regulate the activity of a pre-existing pool of PUMILIO at the level of target engagement.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference about how Norad functions as a buffer.

claim: There are key vulnerable cell populations that become dysfunctional or damaged upon Pum2 induction.
source: This finding raises the question of how transgene induction is able to drive such a striking phenotype if the protein product does not accumulate to supraphysiologic levels. An appealing hypothesis to explain this observation postulates that there are key vulnerable cell populations that become dysfunctional or damaged upon Pum2 induction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the Pum2 transgenic phenotype.

claim: Isolated MEFs from Pum2; rtTA3 transgenic mice show a robust increase in PUM2 protein expression.
source: Indeed, isolated MEFs from Pum2; rtTA3 transgenic mice show a robust increase in PUM2 protein expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), thereby demonstrating clear transgene activity in isolated cell types.
evidence: Western blot data showing PUM2 expression in MEFs is presented in a supplementary figure.

claim: Production of transgenic FLAG-PUM2 is robustly detectable by IHC in Pum2; rtTA3 mice.
source: In addition, given that production of transgenic FLAG-PUM2 is robustly detectable by IHC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), repression of endogenous PUMILIO through a previously described negative feedback mechanism (Galgano et al., 2008; Kedde et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2008) may also contribute to the apparent lack of increase in total PUM2 levels in bulk tissue.
evidence: FLAG IHC data is presented in a supplementary figure, with citations to prior work on PUMILIO feedback regulation.

claim: Repression of endogenous PUMILIO through a negative feedback mechanism may contribute to the apparent lack of increase in total PUM2 levels in bulk tissue of Pum2; rtTA3 mice.
source: In addition, given that production of transgenic FLAG-PUM2 is robustly detectable by IHC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), repression of endogenous PUMILIO through a previously described negative feedback mechanism (Galgano et al., 2008; Kedde et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2008) may also contribute to the apparent lack of increase in total PUM2 levels in bulk tissue.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation with citations to prior work on PUMILIO feedback.

claim: The phenotypic consequences of PUMILIO hyperactivity cannot be attributed to repression of individual targets but rather to the coordinated, modest repression of a broad set of PUMILIO targets in aggregate.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that the absolute magnitude of repression of individual PUM2 targets in Norad–/– or Pum2; rtTA3 tissues is generally low (~10–20%) (for example, see Figure 6). While the complexity of bulk tissue may mask more robust repression of PUM2 targets in specific cell-types, it is likely that the phenotypic consequences of PUMILIO hyperactivity cannot be attributed to repression of individual targets. Rather, the coordinated, modest repression of a broad set of PUMILIO targets in aggregate most likely produces the dramatic phenotypes observed.
evidence: This mechanistic interpretation is based on the observed modest repression of individual targets.

claim: Identification of specific cell populations that drive aging-associated phenotypes under conditions of Norad-deficiency or PUMILIO hyperactivity may reveal new cell types whose dysfunction contributes to the natural aging-associated decline of tissue homeostasis and renewal.
source: Identification of specific cell populations that drive aging-associated phenotypes under conditions of Norad-deficiency or PUMILIO hyperactivity represents an important priority for future work as this approach may reveal new cell types whose dysfunction contributes to the natural aging-associated decline of tissue homeostasis and renewal.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions and potential implications.
